title: Canada gives federal map drawing to independent commissions
body: After each 10-year census, independent electoral boundaries commissions in Canada's provinces redraw their federal electoral districts. The process takes account of changes in population and in the distribution of seats.
takeaway: An election law can assign drawing the boundaries to people who are independent of those contesting the seats.
visual: a plain map with fine district lines on a commission meeting table

title: Swiss constitutional changes need two majorities
body: A Swiss constitutional amendment needs a majority of the national popular vote and a majority in the tally of cantonal votes. A canton is a member state of the Swiss federation, and some count as half a vote.
takeaway: A proposal can win more votes nationwide and still fail the regional test.
source: SWI swissinfo.ch, How Swiss Direct Democracy Works
visual: a ballot box before a relief map of Switzerland with regional boundaries

title: In the UN General Assembly, every country gets one vote
body: Article 18 of the UN Charter gives each member state one vote in the General Assembly, irrespective of population. The charter sets a two-thirds majority of members present and voting for important questions, including votes on the budget.
takeaway: Counting states equally answers a different question from counting each of their residents equally.
visual: an arc of equally spaced empty desks in a large assembly hall
